transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-07-12
Start: 16:00 UTC
Duration: 52 minutes
Attendees: Michael Chen (Redwood AE), Priya Nair (Redwood SE), Carlos Ruiz (Redwood SE), Lena Ortiz (CTO, Quasar Fitness), Ravi Patel (ML Eng), Sam Brooks (Product), Tanya Gomez (Security), Ben Wu (Infra)

--- Optional auto summary (auto):
Quasar is building an at-scale personalized coaching assistant embedded in their apps. They need ~30k token context to stitch long workout histories + medical notes, support for English + Spanish + Portuguese, and safe tool-calling into booking/payments/catalog APIs. They are weighing hosted (fast), dedicated (predictable), and private (compliance) options.

00:00 Michael Chen (Redwood AE): Hey everyone, thanks for taking the time. Quick roll call, then Priya will do a short tech run-through.
00:18 Lena Ortiz (CTO): Hi, Lena here. Excited to dig in.
00:22 Ravi Patel (ML Eng): Ravi, hi.
00:27 Sam Brooks (Product): Sam here.
00:30 Tanya Gomez (Security): Tanya on security.
00:33 Ben Wu (Infra): Ben on infra.
00:36 Michael: Great. Priya over to you?
00:40 Priya Nair (Redwood SE): Cool, thanks. So our goal is to map your workload to model and runtime choices. First, quick on context length: what are you seeing in production prompt sizes?
00:55 Ravi: We're stitching multiple sources — last 12 months of sessions, health notes — so the effective context per request can be 20k to 40k tokens depending on user. Average is around 18k but tail hits 30k.
01:12 Priya: Ok so long context is real. We often recommend profiling tail behavior and maybe truncating less relevant history, but Redwood supports model variants and runtimes that go to 32k and above with split-KV strategies. Quick note, sorry the transcript sometimes says K V cash, that's the engine's K V cache.
01:33 Carlos Ruiz (Redwood SE): Also, for 30k+ you want to watch tokenization differences — Spanish/Portuguese compress differently, so effective token count varies.
01:46 Sam Brooks: Right, we saw Spanish texts were denser so token counts were slightly lower in testing which helped, but Portuguese was noisier.
01:58 Michael: On model choice — are you leaning open models or considering API-first models? What's the tolerance for fine-tuning / RLHF?
02:08 Lena: We prefer open models for cost and control, and we want to host on dedicated or private if the compliance bar pushes us. Fine-tuning isn't first priority; mostly prompt engineering and tool-calling.
02:21 Priya: Good, that aligns. For open models we typically evaluate Llama-3 family, Mistral 2, and some MPT variants; then consider 4-bit/8-bit quantized builds for latency/cost. Any models you already benchmarked?
02:36 Ravi: We ran a small set locally — Llama-3-8B, gemini-lite (customer notes said this) and Mistral-v2, but the quantized runtime was noisy, so we haven't settled. Our bigger question is function-calling reliability: we need deterministic structured outputs for booking APIs.
02:56 Carlos: Redwood's function/tool-calling supports structured schemas and retries. We'll also attach schema validation on our side; if model hallucination is a problem we can run a reranker or a small validation model. Also note: in private deployments, per-customer KMS keys can be configured.
03:18 Tanya (Security): On KMS, does Redwood support HSM-backed keys and bring-your-own-key across hosted and private?
03:26 Michael: Hosted supports customer-managed keys in the cloud provider KMS for enterprise tiers; private supports on-prem HSM integrations. We'll send the exact KMS/HSM matrix.
03:40 Tanya: We need SOC2 docs and proof of encryption in-flight and at rest, plus SSO via SAML and fine-grained RBAC. Auditing is key.
03:49 Carlos: Yes, we have audit logs per request and can export them to your SIEM. We'll include that in the security pack.
04:02 Ben (Infra): For private, how invasive is the package? We have strict network segmentation and say, no outbound except to a fixed Redwood control plane endpoint.
04:13 Priya: Private offers a customer-managed control plane and you can lock egress via VPC peering and NAT rules. We'll map requirements in the VPC diagram.
04:26 Sam: Switching back to models — for long context are there sweet spots? Do we pick a 13B with extended context or a 70B baseline?
04:36 Priya: There's a tradeoff — larger models typically generalize better for instruction and tool-calling but cost more. For deterministic structured outputs sometimes a smaller tuned model can be better. Redwood Optimize can recommend quantization and batching settings per model.
04:56 Ravi: Latency target for user-facing flows is sub-800ms 95p for short replies, but for long-context synthesis we can accept 2 to 3 seconds median; cost is a big factor though.
05:12 Priya: For 30k context that's going to add tokens processed; we advise selective caching for static parts of the history, and prefix caching for common system prompts. That can reduce cost and latency significantly.
05:29 Michael: A quick note on pricing: hosted is per-token; dedicated mixes committed throughput and lower unit rates; private has a platform/seat cost — we'll sketch numbers after this call.
05:43 Ravi: Cool. On multilingual — are there recommended tokenizers or model families for Spanish + Portuguese?
05:49 Priya: Models trained on multilingual corpora like some Llama-3 variants and MPT-xx can be strong; we often see Mistral variants perform well on Romance languages. But tokenization and subword splits matter — we'll run your prompts through tokenizer to give effective token counts.
06:07 Carlos: We'll need your sample prompts and a small dataset to run the 5k-30k token perf tests. Ravi, can you share that?
06:13 Ravi: Yes, I'll upload to the secure bucket after the call.
06:16 Michael: Great.
06:18 06:18 Michael: (note: slight bleed in audio) Next up — tool-calling. What are the APIs you need to call and what's the expected safety model?
06:31 Sam: Mainly booking, pricing, and access-check APIs. We need structured JSON back from the model to call our endpoints, plus verification steps so it doesn't overstep.
06:43 Priya: Redwood's function calling works with a declared schema; we can run a verification step that checks fields, types, and ranges before submitting. We also support signing/nonce patterns for actions.
06:58 Tanya: Will logs contain PII? We need redaction at rest for certain payloads.
07:05 Carlos: We can configure token-level redaction and PII scrubbing or ensure those fields are never persisted in the control plane for private. For hosted, we have options for retention windows.
07:18 Ben: What about fallback behavior? If model fails or latency spikes, how do we handle graceful degradation?
07:25 Priya: You can configure smart routing — fallback to a smaller model or preserved cache. Redwood can do region failover and model-variant fallback. We'll walk through a sample policy.
07:38 Lena: Ok, the procurement/legal side wants to know about data residency — EU data must remain in EU. Do you provide region pinning for hosted?
07:46 Michael: Yes, we have regional hosting choices and can pin model inference to regions; for strict residency we usually recommend private or dedicated with region-specific clusters.
07:58 Tanya: Are there known quirks when using quantized models with long context? Any instability in tool-calling?
08:06 Priya: Quantization can sometimes affect tokenization-sensitive tasks; we do A/B tests. For critical tool-calling we often keep the caller model at higher precision and quantize less-critical assist models. We'll test that in the perf run.
08:22 Ravi: Regarding model flavors, is it straightforward to swap model backends if one fails accreditation? We need rollbacks.
08:29 Carlos: Yes, rollouts are supported with canary and automatic fallback. You can pin versions and run A/B.
08:36 Sam: For the POC, we'd like a mix: hosted trial for speed, dedicated reserved capacity estimate, and a private on-prem proof for compliance. Is that feasible in parallel?
08:48 Michael: Yes, parallel tracks are possible. We'll size the dedicated pool and outline the private packaging effort. But private usually has longer lead-time.
08:57 Priya: For the perf checks, recommended approach: provide 50 representative sessions across languages and tail-size examples; we'll run them on three model candidates and provide logs (latency, tokens, cost estimate).
09:12 Ravi: We'll add edge cases like corrupted input and overly long sequences.
09:19 Michael: Great. Any blockers from legal/or infra?
09:23 Tanya: Need to review DPA and encryption keys options. Also an incident response runbook is handy.
09:30 Carlos: We'll attach our standard DPA template and IR procedures.
09:36 Ben: For private deployment, is there a supported list of hardware and GPUs? We run on-prem with a mix of A100 and H100.
:09:47 Priya: Both supported; our runtime has hardware-specific kernel selection. We'll send the exact compatibility matrix.
09:55 Lena: That sounds good. On timeline, we're aiming for a pilot in Q4; procurement wants a clear budget by end of July.
10:04 Michael: We'll prioritize pricing sketch by 7/15.
10:07 Priya: Quick action: Ravi please share prompts and a dockerfile-ish infra notes if you have them.
10:12 Ravi: Will do today.
10:14 10:14 Carlos: One more technical caveat — long-context retrieval is often cheaper than keeping everything in prompt. Have you looked at hybrid retrieval + short prompt summarizations?
10:25 Sam: We discussed RAG already; we like it but worried about consistency for sequential session state.
10:33 Priya: You can use cached session vectors for quick retrieval and then append a small summary; Redwood supports prefix caching to speed that.
10:44 Michael: Ok let's recap and commit next steps.
10:47 Michael: Recap: Redwood to send pricing sketch and hosted/dedicated/private deltas; SE to run perf tests on 3 candidate models using your prompts; security docs and KMS details to be shared; Quasar to provide prompt set. Follow-up meeting to review perf results and decide POC path.
11:12 Lena: That works. If we can get the security pack quickly we can fast-track procurement.
11:20 Tanya: Yup, security review first.
11:24 Michael: Thanks everyone, we'll follow up with the items.
11:29 Meeting end.
